HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  This is a 78-year-old gentleman
who presented to the cardiac catheterization laboratory after
being referred for approximately three episodes of chest pain
while walking followed by a positive exercise tolerance test.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  The past medical history was
significant for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia,
noninsulin dependent diabetes mellitus, a positive family
history, bilateral claudication, carotid stenosis, prostatic
cancer treated with radiation therapy, glaucoma and a right
inguinal hernia repair.  The patient also stated that he had
a transient ischemic attack with one episode of loss of
speech; however, this resolved spontaneously after two
minutes with no further symptoms following this episode.

ALLERGIES:  There were no known drug allergies.

MEDICATIONS ON ADMISSION:
Glucovance 1.25 mg/250 mg p.o. q.d.
Plavix 75 mg p.o. q.d.
Xanax 0.5 mg p.o. p.r.n. for anxiety.
Pravachol 40 mg p.o. q.d.
Toprol XL 50 mg p.o. q.d.
Aspirin 81 mg p.o. q.d.

LABORATORY DATA ON ADMISSION:  Laboratory values on admission
to the hospital were unremarkable with the exception of a
blood glucose level of 259.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION ON ADMISSION:  The patient's physical
examination on admission was also unremarkable with stable
vital signs.

HOSPITAL COURSE:  The patient was taken to the cardiac
catheterization laboratory and underwent a cardiac
catheterization, which revealed a left ventricular ejection
fraction of 55% and a left main coronary artery occlusion of
90% as well as three vessel coronary artery disease.  He was
taken to the operating room as a result of these
catheterization findings on [**2116-8-7**], where underwent
coronary artery bypass grafting times four with a left
internal mammary artery graft to the left anterior descending
artery, a saphenous vein graft to the obtuse marginal artery,
a saphenous vein graft to the posterior descending artery and
a saphenous vein graft to the first branch of the diagonal
artery.

Postoperatively, the patient was transported from the
operating room to the cardiac surgery recovery unit on
intravenous nitroglycerin and propofol drip.  He remained
intubated until postoperative day #1 due to slightly excess
amounts of postoperative bleeding and coagulopathy, which
were corrected over the first 12 to 18 hours.

On postoperative day #1, the patient was weaned from the
mechanical ventilator and extubated.  He was noted to be in
atrial fibrillation and was started on intravenous amiodarone
drip and Lopressor.  As he became to become more awake, the
patient was noted to be extremely confused, agitated and
occasionally combative, requiring sedation at times.
Diuresis was initiated.

On postoperative day #3, there was a concern for aspiration
due to excessive coughing noted when the patient was given
any oral medication.  The patient was evaluated by the speech
therapist, who felt that the patient was at high risk for
aspiration and a nasogastric tube was inserted to initiate
nutritional support during this time.

There was a question of an aspiration pneumonia.  Although
this was not evident by chest x-ray, the patient had a lot of
respiratory secretions with a significant cough and a bit of
an elevated white blood cell count and it was felt prudent to
place him on empiric antibiotic therapy of levofloxacin and
Flagyl to cover him for possible aspiration pneumonia.  The
only significant chest x-ray finding over the few days were
bilateral pleural effusions.

The patient remained in the cardiothoracic intensive care
unit over the next few days essentially for close monitoring,
pulmonary toilet issues and control of atrial fibrillation.
He was transferred to the telemetry floor out of the
intensive care unit on postoperative day #5.  The patient was
noted to be very agitated and combative at that time and he
was also back in rapid atrial fibrillation.  This was treated
with intravenous Lopressor.  The patient was given some
sedation as well as soft restraints for the patient's safety.

Over the next few days, the patient remained hemodynamically
stable in atrial fibrillation.  His pulmonary status was
marginal, partly due to his mental status and inability to
cooperate with pulmonary toilet efforts.  He was begun on low
dose Coumadin for anticoagulation for his atrial
fibrillation.  The patient was slow to progress over the next
few days with physical therapy.

The patient's other concern over these few days was his blood
sugar, which was very difficult to control.  The [**Hospital **]
Clinic was consulted and assisted with glucose control.

The patient was maintained with nasogastric tube feedings
over the time that he continued to be an aspiration risk.
The speech therapy service continued to follow the patient
regularly.  The patient went for a video swallow study on
postoperative day #7, which revealed no aspiration at that
time, simply delayed swallowing.  It was the speech
therapist's recommendation to begin an oral diet with a
pureed diet and honey-thick liquids and avoidance of thin
liquids.  This was initiated and the patient tolerated this
without problems.

On [**2116-8-18**], postoperative day #11, the patient continued to
have marginal respiratory status with intermittent episodes
of tachypnea and hypoxia.  A chest x-ray was obtained that
showed bilateral effusions, left greater than right, and a
left thoracentesis was performed.  The patient improved
clinically and his followup chest x-ray revealed no
pneumothorax and significant resolution of the pleural
effusion.

On postoperative day #13, [**2116-8-20**], the patient remained
hemodynamically stable.  He was in atrial fibrillation with a
controlled ventricular rate.  His pulmonary status was much
more stable than it had been.  He had a good, strong cough.
Another chest x-ray was obtained for surveillance purposes
and this revealed small bilateral pleural effusions without
other significant x-ray findings.  The patient's mental
status had completely cleared and he was alert and oriented
and it was felt appropriate to screen him for rehabilitation
placement at this time.  It was also noted at this time that
the patient was somewhat dehydrated by laboratory values with
a sodium of 147 and a BUN of 50 and the patient was given
more fluids at that time.

Today, [**2116-8-21**], postoperative day #14, the patient remains
hemodynamically stable.  He is stable from a pulmonary
standpoint and is ready to be discharged to a rehabilitation
facility.

VITAL SIGNS ON DISCHARGE:  The patient has a temperature of
95.5??????F, a pulse of 66 in atrial fibrillation, a respiratory
rate of 22, a blood pressure of 130/60 and a room air oxygen
saturation of 95%.

LABORATORY DATA ON DISCHARGE:  The most recent laboratory
values today are as follows:  a white blood cell count of
11,900, hematocrit of 26.3 and platelet count of 379,000.
The prothrombin time is 19.9 and the INR is 2.6.  There is a
sodium of 146 (which is down from 147 on [**2116-8-20**]), potassium
of 4.2, chloride of 107, bicarbonate of 29, BUN of 44 (which
was down from 50 yesterday), creatinine of 1.1 and blood
glucose of 55 this morning (which has come up with oral
juice.)

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION ON DISCHARGE:  Neurologically, the
patient is alert and oriented, without apparent neurologic
deficit.  On pulmonary examination, the patient has coarse
rhonchi bilaterally with a few bibasilar crackles, left
greater than right.  The patient has a productive cough.  His
room air oxygen saturation is 95%.  The patient is in atrial
fibrillation, S1 and S2, without murmur.  The sternum is
stable.  The incision is intact with no drainage.  The
staples to the incision show no drainage or erythema.  The
abdominal examination is benign.  The patient is tolerating
his oral intake without problem.  [**Name (NI) **] is urinating
spontaneously.  Peripherally, the patient has warm
extremities with palpable pulses.  The left leg incision has
a small amount of serosanguinous drainage around the
incision.

q.i.d.

on b.i.d. insulin and his tube feeds were discontinued, his

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS FOLLOWING BELOW KNEE AMPUTATION

This information is designed as a guideline to assist you in a
speedy recovery from your surgery. Please follow these
guidelines unless your physician has specifically instructed you
otherwise. Please call our office nurse if you have any
questions. Dial 911 if you have any medical emergency.

ACTIVITY:

There are restrictions on activity. On the side of your
amputation you are non weight bearing for 4-6 weeks. You should
keep this amputation site elevated when ever possible.

No driving until cleared by your Surgeon.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

Redness in or drainage from your leg wound(s).

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR.

Exercise:

Limit strenuous activity for 6 weeks.

Do not drive a car unless cleared by your Surgeon.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next 14 days.

Try to keep leg elevated when able.

BATHING/SHOWERING:

You may shower immediately upon coming home. No bathing. A
dressing may cover you??????re amputation site and this should be
left in place for three (3) days. Remove it after this time and
wash your incision(s) gently with soap and water. You will have
sutures, which are usually removed in 4 weeks. This will be done
by the Surgeon on your follow-up appointment.

WOUND CARE:

Sutures / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for staple
removal.

When the sutures are removed the doctor may or may not place
pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision. These will
stay on about a week and you may shower with them on. If these
do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off with warm
water and soap in the shower.

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for
four weeks after surgery.

MEDICATIONS:

Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the
medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a
new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every
three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small
balanced meals throughout the day.

CAUTIONS:

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

Avoid pressure to your amputation site.

No strenuous activity for 6 weeks after surgery.

DIET:

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively.
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent
meals may be preferred.

For people with vascular problems we would recommend a
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred
or get a referral from your doctor.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get
a referral from your doctor.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may
request a referral from your doctor.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT:

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated!

Please call the office on the first working day after your
discharge from the hospital to schedule a follow-up visit. This
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days
after discharge. Normal office hours are 8:30-5:30 Monday
through Friday.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE.
